author: Carlos Martinez
title: Pedal Spacing and Angle Setup for Consistent Braking
description: Foot position drives braking consistency. Learn to set pedal spacing, angle, and height for repeatable pressure and smooth stops.

sections.p: A half-inch shift in foot position kills braking consistency. Your pedal spacing, angle, and height determine whether your heel sits solidly in a fixed location or slides and rotates with each lap. When the foot moves between pedal engagements, trail braking becomes guesswork, lock-ups multiply, and lap times scatter. The fix is not harder braking—it is a rigid foot geometry that lets muscle memory take over.

This guide covers the hardware setup that makes braking repeatable: spacing between pedal centers, pedal angle relative to the floor, and height relative to your hip and seat back. These are the first adjustments to make before you touch brake gain, peak power, or any load cell tuning.

sections.h2: Why pedal geometry matters for consistency

sections.p: Braking is muscle memory. A load cell pedal measures force, not travel, so the only feedback you get is what your foot feels during the press. If your foot lands in a different spot each lap, the pressure curve feels different even if the hardware is identical. A quarter-inch vertical shift changes the angle of your ankle. A half-inch lateral drift rotates your foot on the pedal face. Both alter the initial pressure ramp and make threshold braking unrepeatable.

Spacing between brake and throttle is critical. Too narrow (less than 4 inches, or about 10 cm) and your foot cannot move cleanly between pedals without your heel lifting or your toes brushing both. Too wide (more than 7 inches) and transition braking requires excessive lateral foot movement, which destabilizes your ankle and slows down pedal changes. The sweet spot for most drivers is 5 to 6.5 inches (12.7 to 16.5 cm), measured center-to-center.

Start by measuring the distance between the brake and throttle pedal centers with a ruler or caliper. Place the baseline measurement while the pedals are mounted in their factory position or at their current angle. This is your reference point; do not adjust both pedals simultaneously without documenting the original state.

list: Narrow spacing (4 to 5 inches): easier for quick transitions, less lateral foot movement, but leaves little margin if your foot rolls. Best for rally or street-circuit driving where pedal changes are frequent.
Medium spacing (5.5 to 6.5 inches): the most common range; balances transition speed with foot stability and heel clearance. Suits most iRacing drivers and road-racing series.
Wide spacing (7+ inches): maximizes stability and heel room but requires large foot movements and slower transitions. Rarely necessary unless you have very large feet or a very tall cockpit.

sections.p: If you are building your first load cell pedal setup, most pedal plates and mounting brackets allow 1 to 2 inches of lateral adjustment before you reach the limits of the bolt holes. Make one small change at a time, then do a 10-lap test before moving again. A consistent spacing usually takes two or three iterations.

sections.h2: Pedal angle and the tilting question

sections.p: The angle of each pedal face relative to the floor affects where your foot makes contact and how pressure builds. A typical factory setup tilts the brake pedal 10 to 20 degrees away from vertical, so you press downward and slightly backward. Some drivers tilt the pedal even more (up to 30 degrees) for a shallower engagement curve; others prefer a near-vertical setup for a more direct pressure ramp.

The throttle usually sits at a shallower angle (5 to 15 degrees) or nearly flat, because the throttle requires lighter touches and faster modulation. When the throttle angle matches the brake angle, your foot transitions in a single motion. When they differ significantly, your ankle must rotate between pedals, which adds milliseconds and variability to your shift time.

list: Near-parallel brake and throttle (within 5 degrees of each other): foot moves in a simple lateral slide; fastest and most consistent for threshold braking and quick heel-toe.
Throttle flatter than brake (5 to 10 degree difference): natural for drivers who prefer a relaxed throttle feel and more aggressive brake angle; common in oval racing setups.
Brake significantly angled (30+ degrees) and throttle flat: extreme but workable if your leg length and seat position allow clean transitions without heel or toe contact.

sections.p: Most drivers report the best consistency when brake and throttle angles are within 10 degrees of each other. Experiment by adjusting the brake angle first. Rotate it a few degrees steeper or shallower, then test 10 to 15 laps at a familiar track to feel the difference in pressure onset and transition smoothness.

Pedal height is the vertical distance from the floor to the top of the pedal face, measured when the pedal is at rest. Depth is how far forward or backward the pedals sit relative to your hip and seat. Together they determine your leg angle and whether you can keep a flat foot throughout the braking stroke.

When the pedal is too low, your knee bends excessively and your ankle dorsiflexes (toes point upward), which forces you to push with your calf rather than your whole leg. You lose stability and fine control. When the pedal is too high, your leg extends too far, your heel lifts off the platform, and even small adjustments feel abrupt.

The ideal setup has your heel on the floor throughout the braking stroke, your knee bent at roughly 90 degrees, and your toes pointing slightly downward (about 10 to 20 degrees below horizontal). This position lets you apply force through your whole leg and adjust pressure with small ankle movements.

list: Measure the height from the floor to the pedal face when the pedal is at rest (no pressure applied).
Sit in your racing position with your seat, back, and headrest locked in place. Your heel should be roughly 1 to 2 inches behind the pedal platform.
Check that your leg angle feels natural at full brake pressure. You should not feel cramped or extended.
Adjust pedal depth (fore-aft position) so that you can reach the pedal without leaning forward or stretching your leg past comfortable extension.

sections.tip: Take a photo of your foot position during braking (from the side if you can) and compare it lap to lap. If your heel lifts, your toes curl, or your knee angle changes, your height or depth setting needs adjustment. Consistency in foot geometry is the foundation for consistent brake feel.

sections.p: Once you have set spacing, angle, and height, do a baseline test at a track you know well. Run 10 to 15 laps at a steady pace, focusing on braking into the same turn every lap. Record your pedal telemetry if your sim records it (most iRacing tools do). Look for variation in peak brake pressure, pressure rise rate, or the point in the braking zone where you reach threshold.

If your brake pressure scatter is high (more than a 50 N difference lap to lap), your foot geometry is still fighting you. Make one change at a time: adjust spacing by a quarter-inch, or angle by 2 degrees, then repeat the test. Small, deliberate moves reveal which adjustment has the biggest impact on your consistency.

After three or four sessions, your foot should find the same spot every lap without thinking. Your peak pressure should vary by no more than 20 to 30 N across 10 clean laps. Once that happens, you can move on to fine-tuning load cell gain, brake force curve, or pedal play. Geometry first, software second.

list: Spacing too narrow: forces your heel to lift or your foot to twist when moving between pedals. Increase spacing by half an inch and test again.
Brake pedal too flat (near-vertical): reduces the mechanical advantage of your leg and makes small pressure changes feel jerky. Tilt the brake pedal 15 to 20 degrees away from vertical.
Pedal height too low: causes your knee to bend excessively and your heel to lift off the platform. Raise the pedal by an inch or adjust your seat forward.
Throttle angle too different from brake: forces your ankle to rotate between pedals, slowing transitions and adding variability. Keep them within 10 degrees.
No heel platform: some budget setups lack a footrest or heel block. Add one with wood, aluminum angle, or a purpose-built plate so your heel stays fixed throughout the braking stroke.

sections.h2: Pedal spacing with different car types

sections.p: Different cars feel different partly because of how drivers adjust their setup. In open-wheel cars with heel-toe downshifting, many drivers prefer slightly narrower spacing (5 to 5.5 inches) to speed up throttle-brake transitions. In GT and touring cars, where heel-toe is less critical, spacing of 6 to 6.5 inches is common. Oval racers sometimes run wider spacing because of the lower pedal change frequency.

The core principle remains the same: your foot should land in the same spot every lap, no matter the car. If you notice your braking is inconsistent after switching cars, check spacing and angle before you blame the car's brake response.

Once your pedal geometry is locked in, you can confidently adjust load cell gain, peak force, and brake force curve. These software settings will now affect your feel reliably because your foot position is stable. A higher gain setting on a poorly spaced pedal feels chaotic; the same gain on a well-tuned geometry feels responsive and natural.
For more detail on load cell tuning after your spacing is set, see the guide to load cell pedal setup. The key sequence is geometry first, then software.

faqs.q: What is the ideal brake-to-throttle spacing?
faqs.a: Most drivers find 5.5 to 6.5 inches (center-to-center) optimal. Narrower spacing (5 inches) speeds up transitions but leaves less margin for foot slip. Wider spacing (7 inches) improves stability but slows pedal changes. Start at 6 inches and adjust by half-inch increments based on how your transitions feel over 10-lap tests.

faqs.q: Should my brake and throttle pedals be at the same angle?
faqs.a: They should be within 5 to 10 degrees of each other. This lets your foot transition smoothly without rotating your ankle. If your brake is tilted 20 degrees and your throttle is nearly flat, the rotation between pedals adds milliseconds and variability. Experiment by matching their angles first, then adjust if comfort requires it.

faqs.q: How do I know if my pedal height is correct?
faqs.a: Sit in your racing position with your heel on a footrest behind the pedal platform. At full brake pressure, your knee should be bent about 90 degrees and your heel should remain on the platform without lifting. If your heel lifts or your knee fully extends, raise the pedal or move your seat back. If your knee is too bent, lower the pedal or move your seat forward.

faqs.q: Can bad pedal geometry be fixed in software?
faqs.a: No. Poor spacing, angle, or height causes your foot to land in different positions each lap. No amount of gain adjustment or curve tuning will make a moving target consistent. Fix your geometry first, then tune software. You will see immediate improvement in braking scatter and consistency.
